body.p: The Office Action mailed April 22, 2024 (hereinafter "Office Action") has been carefully reviewed, and Applicant respectfully requests reconsideration of the rejections of Applicant's claims, particularly in view of the foregoing amendments and the remarks that follow.
Claims 1 and 4-13 were previously pending. By the present submission, claims 1, 5, 10, 11, and 13 have been amended, and claim 4 has been cancelled.

Claim 1 has been amended to incorporate the subject matter of cancelled claim 4, to replace the term "apply a torque to at least one wheel of the actuator" with "apply the torque to the at least one wheel of the vehicle," to replace "is above zero" with "is greater than zero," to replace "is below zero" with "is less than zero," and to add the clause "control the actuator to generate the desired torque on the at least one wheel" at the end.
Claim 5 has been amended to replace "one of the wheels" with "one wheel of a plurality of wheels."

Claim 10 has been amended to replace "and indicative" with "and the control signal being further indicative," to replace "is above zero" with "is greater than zero," to replace "is below zero," with "is less than zero, the control signal being further indicative of an offset wheel speed parameter when a wheel speed for the vehicle is less than a threshold vehicle speed limit," to add a single comma, and to replace the term "transmit an actuator signal to the actuator for the actuator" with "control the at least one actuator."
Claim 11 has been amended to replace "the vehicle transmission" with "a vehicle transmission."

Claim 13 has been amended to incorporate the subject matter of cancelled claim 4, to replace "is above zero" with "is greater than zero," to replace "is below zero" with "is less than zero," and to add a single comma.

The amendments to Applicant's claims are fully supported by and consistent with the originally filed specification. No new matter within the meaning of 35 U.S.C. § 132(a) and 37 C.F.R. § 1.121 has been introduced by the foregoing amendments.

body.p: In the Office Action at paragraph 5, claim 1 was provisionally rejected on the ground of nonstatutory double patenting as being unpatentable over claim 3 of co-pending U.S. Patent Application No. 17/758,679 in view of U.S. Patent Application Publication No. 2021/0370779 Al to Ford (hereinafter, "Ford").

While noting the double patenting rejection, Applicant respectfully requests the outstanding double patenting rejection be held in abeyance until such a time as allowable subject matter is identified.

The Office Action noted that a timely filed terminal disclaimer in compliance with 37 C.F.R. § 1.321(c) or 37 C.F.R. § 1.321(d) may be used to overcome a nonstatutory double patenting rejection provided the conflicting patent is shown to be commonly assigned with the present application.

Since both the present application and co-pending Application No. 17/758,679 are still pending and none of the mentioned claims have been allowed, the nonstatutory obviousness-type double patenting rejection is provisional in character. Should these claims from either the present application or co-pending Application No. 17/758,679 become allowed, Applicant reserves the right to file a Terminal Disclaimer or otherwise address the rejection at that time.

p.u: Response to Rejections of Claims 1 and 4-12 Under 35 U.S.C.

body.p: In the Office Action, claims 1 and 4-12 (including independent claims 1 and 10) were rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 101 as being directed to an abstract idea without significantly more (than the judicial exception).
1. Framework of Analysis under 35 U.S.C. § 101
Applicant respectfully disagrees with the foregoing rejections in application to the claims as amended herein, for at least the reasons set out below.

The framework for determining subject matter eligibility for patent claims is summarized in part in a flowchart appearing at MPEP 2103, as modified by the 2019 Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidance (hereinafter, "2019 PEG"), wherein a composite flowchart incorporating the 2019 PEG is set out below.

a practical application by: (1) identifying whether there are any additional elements recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception(s); and (2) evaluating those additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether they integrate the exception into a practical application." (MPEP 21 06.04(d)(II).) In particular:
2106.04(d)(III) (emphasis added).)

The point is echoed in MPEP 2106.05(I), which states that "[e]valuating additional elements to determine whether they amount to an inventive concept requires considering them both individually and in combination to ensure that they amount to significantly more than the judicial exception itself." Because this approach considers all claim elements, the Supreme Court has noted that "it is consistent with the general rule that patent claims 'must be considered as a whole."' Alice Corp., 573 U.S. at 218 n.3, 110 USPQ2d at 1981 (quoting Diamond v. Diehr, 450 U.S. 175, 188, 209 USPQ 1, 8-9 (1981)). Consideration of the elements in combination is particularly important, because even if an additional element does not amount to significantly more on its own, it can still amount to significantly more when considered in combination with the other elements of the claim. See, e.g., Rapid Litig. Mgmt. v. CellzDirect, 827 F.3d 1042, 1051, 119 USPQ2d 1370, 1375 (Fed. Cir. 2016) (process reciting combination of individually well-known freezing and thawing steps was "far from routine and conventional" and thus eligible); BASCOM Global Internet Servs. v. AT&T Mobility LLC, 827 F.3d 1341, 1350, 119 USPQ2d 1236, 1242 (Fed. Cir. 2016) (inventive concept may be found in the non-conventional and non-generic arrangement of components that are individually well-known and conventional).
2. Patent Eligible Distinctions of Claims 1 and 10

Without conceding the propriety of the analysis under Step 2A, Prong 1 and solely to expedite prosecution, Applicant will assume arguendo that independent claims 1 and 10 recite an abstract idea as noted in the Office Action.

With respect to the analysis under Step 2A, Prong 2, Applicant asserts that claims 1 and 10, as amended, recite additional limitations that integrate the judicial exception into a practical application. Namely, claim 1 has been amended to recite, among other things, "control the actuator to generate the operating torque on the at least one wheel." Similarly, claim 10 has been amended to recite, among other things, "control the at least one actuator to generate the operating torque on the at least one wheel without exceeding the actuator rotational speed limit."

Both claims 1 and 10 have been amended to include limitations corresponding to independent claim 13 (which has been found to be patent eligible by the Office Action). As noted in the Office Action at the top of page 13, claim 13 recites the limitation "controlling the actuator

to generate the operating torque on the at least one wheel without exceeding the actuator rotational speed limit," which the Office Action found to integrate the subject matter to an actual and practical implementation of a specific use. Therefore, similar to claim 13, Applicant respectfully submits that claims 1 and 10, as amended, now recite a practical implementation of the abstract idea under at least Step 2A, Prong 2 of the analysis; and are therefore patent eligible.

For at least the foregoing reasons, claims 1 and 10 are directed to patent-eligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. 101, such that the rejections of such claims should be withdrawn. All claims depending from claims 1 and 10 are patent eligible for at least the same reasons articulated above in connection with claims 1 and 10.
Withdrawal of all claim rejections under 35 U.S.C. § 101 is respectfully requested.

Applicant respectfully disagrees with the foregoing rejections in application to the claims as amended herein for at least the reasons set out below.

In order for an obviousness rejection to be appropriate, a prior art reference (or references when combined) must typically disclose all of the claim limitations.1 Additionally, "there must be some articulated reasoning with some rational underpinning to support the legal conclusion of obviousness" to establish obviousness.2

The Supreme Court has confirmed that references that teach away from the invention are evidence of the non-obviousness of a claimed invention, and reaffirmed the principle that a fact finder judging patentability "should be aware, of course, of the distortion caused by hindsight bias and must be cautious of arguments reliant upon ex post reasoning."3

Following KSR, the Federal Circuit held that although "rigid" application of the TSM test for obviousness is improper, application of a flexible TSM test remains the primary guarantee against improper "hindsight" analysis, because a flexibly applied TSM test ensures that the obviousness analysis proceeds on the basis of evidence in existence before time the application was filed, as required by 35 U.S.C. § 103.4

A suggestion to combine references cannot require substantial reconstruction or redesign of such references, or a change in basic operating principles of a construction of a reference, to arrive at the claimed invention.5

In considering a reference for its effect on patentability, the reference is required to be considered in its entirety, including portions that teach away from the invention under consideration. Simply stated, the prior art must be considered as a whole.6 "It is impermissible

2 KSR Int'l v. Teleflex, Inc., 550 U.S. 398, 418, 82 USPQ.2d 1385, 1396 (2007).

See also MPEP 2143.01 ("If the proposed modification or combination of the prior art would change the principle of operation of the prior art invention being modified, then the teachings of the references are not sufficient to render the claims prima facie obvious.')

within the framework of section 103 to pick and choose from any one reference only so much of it as will support a given position, to the exclusion of other parts necessary to the full appreciation of what such reference fairly suggests to one of ordinary skill in the art."7 The Federal Circuit and its predecessor court have repeatedly held that if references taken in combination would produce a "seemingly inoperative" device, then such references teach away from the combination and cannot serve as predicates for a primafacie case of obviousness.8

The Federal Circuit has reaffirmed the necessity of avoiding hindsight bias when considering whether a claim may be obvious, noting specifically that a proper obviousness analysis "requires a form of amnesia that 'forgets' the invention and analyzes the prior art and understanding of the problem at the date of invention."9

Turning to paragraphs 14 and 15 (pages 25-26) with respect to previously presented claim 4, the Office Action acknowledged that Ford fails to disclose a determination of a wheel slip limit based on a wheel speed offset parameter; but pointed to Inaguma as teaching a vehicle operating at a low speed utilizing a slip speed as a value to determine control of the vehicle, where the slip speed is corrected if a predetermined value is exceeded (Inaguma Page 3 lines 4-20, Page 6 lines 17-29).

However, it appears that the Office Action has misconstrued the disclosure of Inaguma. In particular, Inaguma discloses calculation of a correction coefficient when the vehicle speed (U) is determined to be in a low speed state (Inaguma, page 3, lines 4-5 and lines 11-12). This correction coefficient is subsequently used to assist in reducing a slip speed (AU) when the slip speed (AU) exceeds a predetermined reference value (page 3 lines 11-14). The reference value is preset such that "the wheel slippage falls within a range that does not significantly reduce the lateral resistance of the tire" (page 3 lines 11-14). In other words, Inaguma does not disclose the calculation of a wheel slip limit based on the vehicle speed (U) and the offset parameter (correction coefficient). Rather, Inaguma teaches the use of a preset reference value so that wheel slippage is maintained within an optimal range to maintain good control of the vehicle.

In contrast to using a preset reference value, amended claims 1 and 13 recite, among other things, "determin[ing] (i.e., in a dynamic manner, as opposed to utilizing a preset value) a wheel slip limit for the at least one wheel of the vehicle based on the offset wheel speed parameter when the wheel speed is less than a threshold vehicle speed limit." Therefore, Ford, Suhre, Gauthier, and Inaguma, whether taken alone or hypothetically in combination, fail to disclose each and every single limitation of amended claims 1 and 13.
For at least the foregoing reasons, Applicant's claims 1 and 13 are non-obvious over Ford, Suhre, Gauthier, and Inaguma, and the rejection of such claim should be withdrawn.

Since dependent claims inherently include the features of the claims on which they depend, claims 5, 7 and 8 (which depend from claim 1) are patentably distinguished over Ford, Suhre, Gauthier, and Inaguma for at least the same reasons articulated above in connection with claim 1.

Accordingly, it is not necessary to address the additional features in dependent claims 5, 7, and 8 to overcome the rejections of such claims; however, Applicant reserves the right to do so in the future, if necessary.
